## Welcome back {.smaller}

- Pre-class: Week 9 reading + GitHub Pre-class Setup
- Quick Instapoll recap — what does a **commit** represent, and how is that different from just saving a file?
- Today: why version control matters, the vocabulary you need, and your first Git-tracked Quarto project

*(0–3 min)*

## Setup Clinic {.smaller}

Before we start: check in with your teammates and make sure that **all** of you have:

1.  A GitHub account
2.  Git installed (Tools \> Global Options \> Git/SVN shows a path)
3.  A working token — run `usethis::git_sitrep()` in the console

If `git_sitrep()` reports a problem, raise your hand — we'll fix it now before it costs you time later.

*(3–10 min)*

## Imagine This... {.smaller}

You ran an analysis a few months ago. A classmate asks for your code. You find three files:

- `analysis.R`
- `analysis_FINAL.R`
- `analysis_FINAL_v2_useThisOne.R`

Which one is actually correct? Do you remember what changed between them? Could you prove it to someone else?

**This is the problem version control solves.**

## What Is Version Control? {.smaller}

> Like "Track Changes" in Google Docs or Word — but for an entire project (code, data, figures, writeups) instead of one document.

It gives you:

- A complete history of **every saved change**
- The ability to go back to **any earlier point**
- A way to share your work so others see **the *same* version** you do

*(10–18 min)*

## Vocabulary: The Core Five {.smaller}

::: incremental
- **Repository (repo):** a project folder that Git is tracking, including its entire history
- **Commit:** a labeled snapshot of your repo at one point in time
- **Remote:** a copy of your repo hosted elsewhere (for us, on GitHub)
- **Push:** send your local commits up to the remote
- **Pull:** bring commits from the remote down to your machine
:::

## The Big Picture {.smaller}

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A[Your laptop<br/>local repo] -- commit --> A
  A -- push --> B[(GitHub<br/>remote repo)]
  B -- pull --> A
```

**Committing** happens **locally** and costs nothing. **Pushing** is the only step that touches **GitHub**.

*(18–26 min)*

## Live Demo: Your First Git-Tracked Project {.smaller}

We'll do this together, live, in a brand-new RStudio Project. **You don't need to type these yet, just watch.**

**1. Create a new Version-Controlled RStudio Project**

File \> New Project \> New Directory \> Quarto Project, check **"Create a git repository"**

- it will ask you to name your directory and choose a home

**2. Confirm Git is tracking the project**

- an error message "can't determine the local repo's default branch" means you have no "commit" yet.

```{r}
#| eval: false
usethis::git_sitrep()
```

## Live Demo (continued) {.smaller}

**3. Write a short Quarto doc** (`demo.qmd`) summarizing the `palmerpenguins` dataset:

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(tidyverse)
library(palmerpenguins)

penguins |>
  count(species)

penguins |>
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g, fill = species)) +
  geom_boxplot()
```

## Live Demo (continued) {.smaller}

**4. Commit the work** — use the RStudio Git pane: check the box next to `demo.qmd`, click **Commit**, write a message like `"Add first penguin summary"`, click **Commit**.

**5. Create a GitHub repo and push, in one step:**

```{r}
#| eval: false
usethis::use_github()
```

**6. View it live on GitHub.com** — refresh the page, see the file, click on it, see the commit history.

*(26–38 min)*

## Wait — Where's My Pretty Report? {.smaller}

You'll notice GitHub shows `demo.qmd` as plain source code, not the rendered report you saw in RStudio.

- **Why:** GitHub's file viewer displays file contents — it doesn't run code or execute HTML for you. That's a deliberate security choice, not a bug.
- Even the `.html` file Quarto renders will show up as raw code on GitHub, not as a live webpage.

**To actually publish the rendered page**: pushes your rendered HTML to a `gh-pages` branch in a public repo. It is **beyond this class** so we will not spend time on this.

```{r}
#| eval: false
quarto publish gh-pages
```

```{=html}
<!-- 
- Run once from the Terminal (or the **blue publish icon** dropdown \> **Publish Document**) in your project folder
- Your repo must be **public** (free GitHub accounts can't publish private repos this way)
- It pushes your rendered HTML to a `gh-pages` branch and opens the live page in your browser automatically

We won't do this together today — optional if you want your project to look like a real website. -->
```

## Your Turn: Guided Practice {.smaller}

Working **on your own machine**, repeat the demo with your own Quarto file:

1.  New Quarto Project with Git enabled (or add Git to an existing project: `usethis::use_git()`)
2.  Create `my_penguins.qmd`. Load `tidyverse` and `palmerpenguins`.
3.  Add **one summary table** (e.g., average bill length by species) and **one plot** of your choosing.
4.  Render the document to check it works.
5.  Commit — **at least twice**, with real messages (e.g., once after the table, once after the plot).
6.  Run `usethis::use_github()` to create your repo and push.
7.  Copy your repo URL and submit it to the Canvas assignment for today's class.

*(38–65 min — ask for help any time!)*

## Common Hiccups {.smaller}

- **"Nothing to commit"** — did you save the file first?
- **Push fails / asks for a password** — your token may not be stored; re-run `gitcreds::gitcreds_set()`
- **Can't find the Git tab in RStudio** — close and reopen the Project after enabling Git
- **`use_github()` errors about an existing repo** — pick a new repo name, or delete the old one on GitHub first

## Wrap-Up {.smaller}

- You now have a real, version-controlled Quarto project on GitHub

A. Push, then commit

B. Commit, then push

C. Pull, then commit

D. Commit only — Git automatically uploads changes
